sup-ffe8871412e77213-q1:whole.hint: Separate what the common small deflections tell you from what the rare large deflections tell you.
notes: Alpha scattering supports a small, dense, positively charged nucleus containing most of the atomic mass. Most particles pass through the largely empty atomic volume.
For a head-on closest-approach calculation, equate the initial kinetic energy to the increase in electric potential energy, using the alpha particle’s charge +2e.

sup-ffe8871412e77213-q3:whole.hint: Find the difference between the two relevant energy levels, not the energy of just one level.
notes: For an atomic transition, photon energy is |E_final − E_initial| = hf = hc/λ. Downward transitions emit; upward transitions require absorption.
Use the positive magnitude of the gap, converting eV to J if using h in SI units. A larger gap corresponds to a shorter wavelength.

sup-07b8e5fb4027154b-w1:e.i.hint: Keep a separate account of nucleon number and electric charge on both sides of the decay.
notes: In alpha decay A decreases by 4 and Z by 2. In beta-minus decay a neutron becomes a proton; in beta-plus decay a proton becomes a neutron, with the appropriate emitted leptons.
Gamma emission changes nuclear energy without changing A or Z. Beta decay shares energy with a neutrino or antineutrino, giving a continuous beta spectrum.
